summary: Defines two IKEv2 Configuration Payload Attribute Types, INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN and INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA, that add support for private, internal-only DNS domains reachable through an IPsec connection. Other domains are resolved as before. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join your company's network, this lets your computer use the company's phone book for company names, and your normal one for everything else.

questions: what is split dns in ikev2
subtitle: How an IKEv2 VPN can tell a client which domain names to look up through the tunnel and which to leave alone.

tldr.problem: A split-tunnel VPN sends only some traffic through the tunnel, yet internal resources often have internal-only DNS names that only internal DNS servers can resolve, and IKEv2 had no standard way to configure this.
tldr.mechanism: Two new IKEv2 Configuration Payload attribute types, INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN (25) and INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA (26), let the responder list the domains for the internal DNS servers to resolve and optionally supply DNSSEC trust anchors for them.
tldr.outcome: Queries for the listed domains go through the tunnel to the internal servers and other queries use the regular resolver. The trust anchors are powerful, so clients must use a whitelist.

today: RFC 8598 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the configuration payload mechanism of RFC 7296.

sections.title: The Split DNS Problem
sections.content:
A split-tunnel VPN sends only packets for a specific destination range, usually chosen from RFC 1918, through the tunnel. Everything else goes straight out. The enterprise does not have to carry its users' unrelated traffic, but the internal resources it offers often have internal-only DNS names that need special internal DNS servers. Split DNS (see RFC 2775) is the usual answer.

The Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2, RFC 7296) negotiates parameters through Configuration Payload attribute types, but it had no standard way to configure Split DNS. Other tunnel protocols already did this, for example through proprietary extensions to IKEv1. This RFC defines two attribute types for IKEv2: INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN says which domain must be resolved with the provided internal DNS servers, and INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA conveys a DNSSEC trust anchor for such a domain.

The trust anchor matters when the public view of a domain uses DNSSEC, which would prove that the internal view does not exist or would expect a different key.
sections.plainLanguage: Only some of your mail goes through the company's mailroom. For company names you need the company's own address book, and this gives your computer a way to learn about it.

sections.title: When It Applies
sections.content:
The attributes apply only to split-tunnel configurations. If the negotiated IPsec connection is not split-tunnel, both attributes MUST be ignored. This keeps generic, non-enterprise VPN services from overriding the public DNS hierarchy, which could lead to malicious overrides of DNS and DNSSEC. Such connections SHOULD use only the existing INTERNAL_IP4_DNS and INTERNAL_IP6_DNS attributes, so all DNS traffic goes through the tunnel and does not leak onto the local network.

An enterprise may use a special domain such as corp.example.com, or run a different version of its public domain internally. In either case the client is told which names are internal and which DNS servers to use. Sending only enterprise queries to the enterprise has two advantages. The enterprise stays unaware of the user's other DNS activity, and its DNS servers need to be configured only for enterprise domains, which removes the legal and technical responsibility of resolving every domain the user might ask for.

Queries for other domains SHOULD go to the client's regular DNS service, unless the client prefers the tunnel for everything, for example on an untrusted network such as a coffee shop or hotel.
sections.plainLanguage: This only makes sense if just some of your traffic goes through the tunnel. If all of it does, you do not need the special list.

sections.title: The Request and Reply Exchange
sections.content:
The initiator signals support by including one or more INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN attributes in its CFG_REQUEST. It then MUST also include INTERNAL_IP4_DNS or INTERNAL_IP6_DNS attributes. The attribute is usually empty but MAY contain a suggested domain. No such attribute means the initiator does not support or will not accept Split DNS. Including INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA signals willingness to receive trust anchors, and then the request MUST also include INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN. An initiator MAY send its current trust anchors for a domain, or a length of 0 if it does not want to.

The responder MAY send INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN attributes in its CFG_REPLY, and if it does it MUST also send one or both of the internal DNS server attributes. If the request included a domain but the reply has none, the initiator MUST behave as if Split DNS is not supported, unless local policy defines default Split DNS domains. Suggested domains in the request MAY be ignored or treated as suggestions.

Each domain MAY be followed by one or more INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA attributes, which MUST immediately follow the domain they apply to. All DNS servers in the reply MUST be able to resolve all listed domains, so the domains form a single list that applies to the whole list of servers.

In the RFC's first example, the responder returns domains example.com and city.other.test with DNS servers 198.51.100.2 and 198.51.100.4. In the second, the initiator also asks for trust anchors and the reply carries two for example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer asks whether there is a special address book for certain names. The company answers with the names and the address of the person to ask, and that is where you send those lookups.

sections.title: The Two Attribute Formats
sections.content:
Multi-octet integers are big-endian. Both attributes begin with a 1-bit Reserved field, a 15-bit Attribute Type and a 2-octet Length.

INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN uses type 25 and its value is a domain name of 0 or more octets: a fully qualified domain name in DNS presentation format, using an IDNA A-label (RFC 5890). Implementors need to be careful that this value is not null terminated.

INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA uses type 26 and is either empty, with Length set to 0, or carries one trust anchor. A non-empty attribute holds a 2-octet DNSKEY Key Tag, a 1-octet DNSKEY Algorithm, a 1-octet Digest Type and one or more octets of Digest Data. The length is 4 octets plus the length of the digest data. The format has no domain name, so it relies on the preceding INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN. Any trust anchor that is not immediately preceded by a domain attribute, or by another trust anchor for the same domain, MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a small header that says what kind it is and how long it is. The body then holds a name, or a fingerprint that proves a name is real.

sections.title: How Clients Apply the Domains
sections.content:
If a reply has no INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN attributes, the client MAY use the provided DNS servers as its default for all queries. A client with local policy limiting accepted domains MUST ignore any others.

For each accepted domain, the client MUST use the provided servers as the only resolvers for that domain and its subdomains, and MUST NOT try the external servers for it. Other names SHOULD be resolved by external resolvers configured independently of IKE. The RFC's example: if the domain is example.test, then www.example.test and mail.eng.example.test go to the internal resolvers, but otherexample.test and ple.test MUST NOT.

The initiator SHOULD allow these domains to resolve to special address ranges such as those of RFC 1918, even if it normally blocks such answers. When the IKE Security Association ends, the DNS forwarding MUST be unconfigured: forwarding rules deleted, cached data for those domains flushed (including negative cache entries), obtained trust anchors removed and the outstanding DNS request queue cleared.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything ending in the company's name goes to the company's address book, and nothing else does. When you leave, your computer forgets all of it.

sections.title: Trust Anchors and the Whitelist
sections.content:
Accepting an INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA trust anchor can be seen as the equivalent of installing an Enterprise CA certificate. It lets the remote IKE server override DNS answers, including DNSSEC signatures, and so potentially confirm or override records such as TLSA (RFC 6698), OPENPGPKEY, SMIMEA or IPSECKEY.

Therefore clients willing to accept trust anchors MUST use a whitelist of one or more domains that can be updated out of band, and a client with an empty whitelist MUST NOT use any. The DNS root zone MUST be ignored if it appears in a whitelist, and other generic or public domains such as TLDs MUST be ignored unless the entity operates the TLD. Whitelist updates MUST come from explicit human interaction or a trusted automated provisioning system. Clients SHOULD accept updates for subdomains of whitelisted names, and MUST ignore trust anchors for any FQDN for which they did not accept a domain attribute.

A recommended policy is to accept trust anchors only for the organization's own DNS names.
sections.plainLanguage: A company-supplied fingerprint can make fake names look real. So your computer only accepts fingerprints for names on a list that you or your admin set up in advance.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If the connection is not split-tunnel, both attributes MUST be ignored, otherwise a generic VPN provider could maliciously override DNSSEC trust anchors of public domains. The configuration relies on the trust established during IKE authentication, so if IKEv2 is negotiated with an anonymous or unknown endpoint, such as for Opportunistic Security (RFC 7435), the initiator MUST ignore Split DNS configuration.

If two connections to different unrelated entities claim the same domain, for example .internal, they MUST NOT be active at the same time. Connections that belong to one organization may share the same values. If a domain is DNSSEC signed in the public view and a domain arrives without a trust anchor, the client SHOULD NOT accept an insecure delegation for domains it did not explicitly request.

Deployments should consider indirect record types such as NS, CNAME, DNAME, MX or SRV. If an MX record for internal.example.com points to mx.internal.example.net, both domains should be listed. Clients MAY want whitelists for TLDs and second-level domains. The content of the attributes may be passed to other programs and SHOULD be treated as untrusted network input.
sections.plainLanguage: Only believe the company's list if you are sure it is really the company. Never let two different companies claim the same name at once.

messages.note: Empty INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN, plus DNS server attributes; optionally INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA.

messages.note: Domains, DNS server addresses, and optionally trust anchors right after each domain.

items.label: INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN
items.desc: Domain to resolve with the internal DNS servers; multi-valued, length 0 or more.

items.label: INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA
items.desc: DNSSEC trust anchor for the preceding domain; multi-valued, length 0 or more.

viz.caption: SIMPLE CASE EXCHANGE FROM RFC 8598 SECTION 3.4.1

data.title: Simple case
data.code:
CP(CFG_REQUEST) =
  INTERNAL_IP4_ADDRESS()
  INTERNAL_IP4_DNS()
  INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS()
  INTERNAL_IP6_DNS()
  INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN()

CP(CFG_REPLY) =
  INTERNAL_IP4_ADDRESS(198.51.100.234)
  INTERNAL_IP4_DNS(198.51.100.2)
  INTERNAL_IP4_DNS(198.51.100.4)
  INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS(2001:DB8:0:1:2:3:4:5/64)
  INTERNAL_IP6_DNS(2001:DB8:99:88:77:66:55:44)
  INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN(example.com)
  INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN(city.other.test)
